passages.t: A dry crust in peace, and the LORD who tests hearts
passages.happening:
‘Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife’ (verse 1). ‘A wise servant will rule over a disgraceful son and share his inheritance as one of the brothers’ (verse 2).

“A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but the LORD is the tester of hearts” (verse 3). ‘He who mocks the poor insults their Maker; whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished’ (verse 5). ‘Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of a son is his father’ (verse 6).

Then a saying about bribes: ‘A bribe is a charm to its giver; wherever he turns, he succeeds’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The Hebrew behind ‘feasting’ in verse 1 is literally sacrifices. The meat at festive meals often came from fellowship offerings, where part of the animal was burned on the altar and the rest eaten by the household. A house full of such meals was a house of plenty and religious celebration. The saying prefers stale bread in quiet to all that abundance soured by quarrels.

Verse 2 is surprising in a world built on inheritance. A wise servant can end up sharing an inheritance with the sons, while a son who disgraces his family loses his place. Character matters more than birth.

Silver and gold were refined in a crucible or furnace that burned off the impurities. The prophets use the same picture of God refining his people. People can test metal. Only the LORD tests hearts.

Verse 5 returns to the poor and their Maker, as 14:31 did. To mock the poor, or to gloat over someone else's disaster, is to insult God.
passages.later: Malachi pictures God at the refiner's fire: ‘And He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver’ (Malachi 3:3). And the law forbids what verse 8 describes: ‘Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous’ (Exodus 23:8).
passages.hard:
Verse 8 says a bribe works like a charm. Is the Bible approving of bribery?

No. This is one of the clearest examples of a proverb that observes instead of commending. Verse 8 describes how a bribe looks from the giver's side: it opens doors and smooths the way. People in the ancient world knew that, as people do now.

But the same chapter condemns ‘A wicked man’ who ‘takes a covert bribe to subvert the course of justice’ (verse 23), and the law forbids bribes outright (Exodus 23:8).

Readers take verse 8 in a few ways. Some hear irony, the briber's own view of his gift, which the reader is meant to see through. Others think it is simply realistic, teaching the young how power works so that they will not be naive. A few scholars distinguish a bribe that bends justice from a gift given to gain a hearing (compare 18:16 and 21:14). On any reading, the book's overall verdict is clear. Justice that can be bought is detestable to the LORD.
passages.asks: The LORD tests hearts the way fire tests silver. Ask what the heat of this season is showing about your heart. And ask whether there is a house you live in, or a table you sit at, where quiet would be worth more than any feast.

passages.t: Covering an offense, and a friend for every season
passages.happening:
‘Whoever conceals an offense promotes love, but he who brings it up separates friends’ (verse 9). ‘A rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool’ (verse 10). ‘It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly’ (verse 12). ‘If anyone returns evil for good, evil will never leave his house’ (verse 13).

“To start a quarrel is to release a flood; so abandon the dispute before it breaks out” (verse 14). Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous are both detestable to the LORD (verse 15).

Then one of the book's best-loved sayings: “A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (verse 17). It is set beside a warning against rashly guaranteeing a neighbor's debt (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Verses 9, 14 and 19 form a thread on quarrels. Verse 14's picture is of water let loose: easy to release, impossible to call back. The wise stop a dispute before it starts.

Covering an offense, as in 10:12, does not mean pretending a wrong never happened, or keeping a crime quiet. It means not keeping a grievance alive by bringing it up again and again.

The Syrian brown bear lived in Israel's hills, and a mother bear robbed of her cubs was proverbial for fury. The saying is funny and serious at once: better to meet her than a fool in the middle of his folly.

Verse 15 is about the courts. Justice was done by elders at the city gate, and the law required judges to acquit the innocent and condemn the guilty (Deuteronomy 25:1). Turning that upside down is detestable to God.

Striking hands in verse 18 was the gesture that sealed a pledge, as a handshake seals an agreement. The man who did it became responsible for his neighbor's debt.
passages.later: The Bible's great friendships show verse 17 in a life. ‘Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as himself’ (1 Samuel 18:3). And Ruth would not leave Naomi in her loss: “For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live” (Ruth 1:16). Paul repeats verse 13: ‘Do not repay anyone evil for evil’ (Romans 12:17).
passages.asks: A friend loves at all times, in hard seasons too. Ask who has been that kind of friend to you, and thank them. And ask who is going through adversity now, and how you could be a brother or sister to them.

passages.t: A joyful heart, and the wisdom of silence
passages.happening:
‘A man fathers a fool to his own grief; the father of a fool has no joy’ (verse 21). “A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones” (verse 22).

‘A wicked man takes a covert bribe to subvert the course of justice’ (verse 23). ‘Wisdom is the focus of the discerning, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth’ (verse 24). ‘A foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him’ (verse 25). ‘It is surely not good to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty’ (verse 26).

The chapter ends with two sayings about restraint. ‘A man of knowledge restrains his words, and a man of understanding maintains a calm spirit’ (verse 27). ‘Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps silent, and discerning when he holds his tongue’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The foolish son of 10:1 comes back in verses 21 and 25. His foolishness is not only his own problem. It is his father's grief and his mother's bitterness. The book is still a father's teaching to a son who will soon have a household of his own.

Verse 22 is honest that a broken spirit affects the whole person, body included. A glad heart is like medicine.

The bribe appears twice in this chapter: described in verse 8, and condemned here in verse 23. Set side by side, the two show how the book teaches. It tells the truth about how the world works, and then it tells the truth about what God thinks of it.

The chapter began with a dry crust in quietness (verse 1) and ends with silence (verse 28). Quiet frames the whole chapter.
passages.later: Job said the same to his talkative friends: “If only you would remain silent; for that would be your wisdom!” (Job 13:5). And Samuel's sons are remembered for the bribe of verse 23: they ‘turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice’ (1 Samuel 8:3).
passages.asks: Even a fool seems wise when he keeps quiet. Ask where you could hold your tongue this week and let silence do more good than words. And ask what has been drying up your spirit, and who could help you find the good medicine of a glad heart again.
